summary: Binary search isn't really about searching arrays — it's about exploiting a monotonic property. If you can answer a yes/no question that flips exactly once across a range, binary search applies.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Is the input (or the answer space) monotonic?
thoughtProcess.body: Sorted arrays are the obvious case. The deeper trick: if you can frame the problem as 'what is the smallest/largest X such that predicate(X) is true?' and predicate is monotonic in X, binary search works on the answer.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. Define the search space precisely.
thoughtProcess.body: low and high must bracket the answer. For BS on answer, low = minimum feasible, high = maximum feasible. Get this wrong and you'll loop forever or miss the answer.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Write a clean predicate / check function.
thoughtProcess.body: Extract the feasibility check into a private boolean method (canPlaceCows, isPaintingCompletionPossible, canBeAllotted). Keep the binary search loop dumb — it just shrinks the range.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. Decide which side to shrink on success.
thoughtProcess.body: Maximize answer (aggressive cows): on success, store result and try larger → low = mid + 1. Minimize answer (painter's partition): on success, store result and try smaller → high = mid - 1. The 'store result on every success' pattern is bulletproof.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Pick the loop invariant: low <= high.
thoughtProcess.body: Default to while (low <= high), exit when low > high, return the stored answer. Avoid low < high unless you have a strong reason — it requires careful mid-update logic.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Watch overflow and types.
thoughtProcess.body: mid = low + (high - low) / 2 — never (low + high) / 2. For mid * mid, use long. For sums (painter, allocate), totals can exceed int.

commonMistakes.title: Mid overflow
commonMistakes.why: low + high can overflow int when both are large. The right form never does.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting to store the candidate answer
commonMistakes.why: When the loop exits, low > high — neither is guaranteed to be the answer. Always capture mid the moment the predicate succeeds.

commonMistakes.title: Wrong direction after success
commonMistakes.wrong:
// Aggressive cows — wanted MAX min distance
if (canPlace(mid)) { ans = mid; high = mid - 1; }
commonMistakes.right: if (canPlace(mid)) { ans = mid; low = mid + 1; } // try larger
commonMistakes.why: Maximize answer → on success go RIGHT. Minimize answer → on success go LEFT. Confuse these and you'll converge to the boundary instead of the optimum.

commonMistakes.title: Off-by-one in lower / upper bound
commonMistakes.wrong:
while (low < high) { ... high = mid; }
// returns... maybe low? maybe -1?
commonMistakes.why: The store-on-success pattern works for both lower and upper bound. Sentinel value handles 'not found' cleanly.

commonMistakes.title: Integer overflow in mid*mid (sqrt)
commonMistakes.right:
long m = mid;
if (m * m <= A) ...
commonMistakes.why: For A up to 1e9, mid can be ~3e4, and mid*mid fits int — but the moment A grows, you blow up silently. Use long up front.

commonMistakes.title: Wrong array bounds in BS on answer
commonMistakes.wrong:
// Painter's: low = 0; high = sum;
// guess time 0 is meaningless and breaks check
commonMistakes.right:
low = max(C[i]);  // can never go below the largest single board
high = sum(C);    // one painter does everything
commonMistakes.why: Pick the tightest valid bounds. Loose bounds waste iterations or trigger predicate bugs.

commonMistakes.title: Rotated array: blindly checking A[mid] == target
commonMistakes.wrong: // Standard BS on rotated array — fails
commonMistakes.why: Rotated arrays break the global sorted invariant. Restore it by finding the pivot or by reasoning about which half is sorted.

commonMistakes.title: Modifying loop variable after store-on-success
commonMistakes.wrong: if (canDo(mid)) { ans = mid; high = mid; }  // not mid - 1
commonMistakes.why: high = mid creates an infinite loop when low == high. With <=, always shrink by 1.

keyPatterns.name: Classic BS on sorted array
keyPatterns.when: You have a sorted array and need to find a specific value or position.

keyPatterns.name: Lower bound (first index with A[i] >= B)
keyPatterns.when: Insertion point, first occurrence, or 'smallest x such that x >= B'.

keyPatterns.name: BS on Answer — minimize the maximum
keyPatterns.when: Partition/allocate so that the largest group is as small as possible.

keyPatterns.name: BS on Answer — maximize the minimum
keyPatterns.when: Place items so that the smallest gap is as large as possible.

keyPatterns.name: BS on value range (count-based)
keyPatterns.when: You can't directly index the answer, but you can count how many items are ≤ X in O(log) or O(N log).

keyPatterns.name: BS on 2D matrix (flattened indexing)
keyPatterns.when: Matrix is globally sorted (next row starts > prev row's end). Treat as 1D, map mid → (mid/M, mid%M).

keyPatterns.name: Peak finding (BS on unimodal)
keyPatterns.when: Function rises then falls (or has a peak property). Always move toward the increasing slope.

keyPatterns.name: Rotated sorted array — find pivot then search
keyPatterns.when: Array is sorted but rotated. Locate the rotation point, then standard BS on the correct half.

edgeCases: N == 1 — answer is A[0] or trivially checkable. Test before entering the loop.
Target smaller than A[0] or larger than A[N-1] — lower/upper bound returns N or -1.
All elements equal — first/last occurrence both span entire array.
Duplicates in 'single element' problem — index parity shifts after the unique element.
Strictly increasing/decreasing arrays in peak problem — peak is at a boundary.
BS on answer with B = 0 — feasibility check must handle 'no operations' cleanly.
Overflow: A up to 1e9 means mid * mid, sum of pages, A * min(B,C) all need long.
Rotated array with rotation = 0 — algorithm should still work without special-casing.
